title: Ζεὺς καὶ Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶ καὶ Μῶμος
part: Zeus, Prometheus, Athena and Momus (Chambry 124 · Perry 100)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 124 (= Perry 100). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς καὶ Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶ κατασκευάσαντες, ὁ μὲν ταῦρον, Προμηθεὺς δὲ ἄνθρωπον, ἡ δὲ οἶκον, Μῶμον κριτὴν εἵλοντο.
sentences.tr: Zeus kai Promētheus kai Athēna kataskeuasantes, ho men tauron, Promētheus de anthrōpon, hē de oikon, Mōmon kritēn heilonto.
sentences.l: Zeus and Prometheus and Athena, having fashioned — the one a bull, Prometheus a man, and she a house — chose Momus as judge.
sentences.i: Zeus and Prometheus and Athena each made a thing — Zeus a bull, Prometheus a man, Athena a house — and chose Momus for judge.
sentences.n: Μῶμος is Blame itself, the personified spirit of fault-finding; Hesiod makes him a child of Night, born beside Distress and Doom. The one participle κατασκευάσαντες governs all three objects at once, and the ὁ μέν … δέ … ἡ δέ series parcels them out afterwards. εἵλοντο is middle: to choose someone for oneself.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ φθονήσας τοῖς δημιουργήμασιν ἀρξάμενος ἔλεγε τὸν μὲν Δία ἡμαρτηκέναι, τοῦ ταύρου τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς κέρασιν μὴ θέντα, ἵνα βλέπῃ ποῦ τύπτει· τὸν δὲ Προμηθέα, διότι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὰς φρένας οὐκ ἔξωθεν ἀπεκρέμασεν, ἵνα μὴ λανθάνωσιν οἱ πονηροί, φανερὸν δὲ ᾖ τί ἕκαστος κατὰ νοῦν ἔχει, τρίτον δὲ ἔλεγεν ὡς ἔδει τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν τὸν οἶκον τροχοῖς ἐπιθεῖναι, ἵνα, ἐὰν πονηρός τις παροικισθῇ γείτων, ῥᾳδίως μεταβαίνῃ.
sentences.tr: Ho de phthonēsas tois dēmiourgēmasin arxamenos elege ton men Dia hēmartēkenai, tou taurou tous ophthalmous epi tois kerasin mē thenta, hina blepēi pou typtei· ton de Promēthea, dioti tou anthrōpou tas phrenas ouk exōthen apekremasen, hina mē lanthanōsin hoi ponēroi, phaneron de ēi ti hekastos kata noun echei, triton de elegen hōs edei tēn Athēnan ton oikon trochois epitheinai, hina, ean ponēros tis paroikisthēi geitōn, rhāidiōs metabainēi.
sentences.l: But he, grudging at the handiworks, made a beginning and said that Zeus had erred in not having set the bull's eyes upon its horns, so that it might see where it strikes; and Prometheus, because he had not hung the man's wits outside, so that the wicked might not escape notice and it might be plain what each man has in mind; and third he said that Athena ought to have set the house on wheels, so that, if some wicked neighbour were settled alongside, one might easily move off.
sentences.i: But Momus, grudging them their handiwork, began and said that Zeus had gone wrong in not putting the bull's eyes on its horns, so that it could see where it was striking; that Prometheus had gone wrong in not hanging a man's wits on the outside of him, so that the bad could not pass unnoticed and it would be plain what each man had in his mind; and third, that Athena ought to have put the house on wheels, so that if a bad neighbour settled next door one could easily move off.
sentences.n: Three faults hang from the one ἔλεγε. The first two are accusative and infinitive, with ἡμαρτηκέναι carried over unspoken to τὸν δὲ Προμηθέα; the third is recast with ὡς and a finite ἔδει, so the sentence changes its own construction halfway. φθονέω with the dative is to look at a thing with a grudging eye. φρένες are the seat of thought, housed in the chest, which is why Momus wants them hung on the outside where they can be read. In the last clause ἵνα … μεταβαίνῃ leaves its subject unspoken: either the house rolls away or the householder does, and the Greek does not decide.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Ζεὺς ἀγανακτήσας κατ’ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ βασκανίᾳ τοῦ Ὀλύμπου αὐτὸν ἐξέβαλεν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho Zeus aganaktēsas kat’ autou epi tēi baskaniāi tou Olympou auton exebalen.
sentences.l: And Zeus, having grown angry at him over his malice, cast him out of Olympus.
sentences.n: ἐπί with the dative gives the ground of the anger. βασκανία is the malice of the evil eye — grudging that wishes harm, not criticism that wants a thing improved. τοῦ Ὀλύμπου is the genitive of the place one is thrown clear of. ἀγανακτήσας κατά again, as with the fox (119).

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐδὲν οὕτως ἐστὶν ἐνάρετον ὃ μὴ πάντως περί τι ψόγον ἐπιδέχεται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti ouden houtōs estin enareton ho mē pantōs peri ti psogon epidechetai.
sentences.l: The story shows that nothing is so excellent as not in every case to admit of blame in some respect.
sentences.n: The relative ὅ with μή is consecutive — 'such as not to' — and the μή rather than οὐ marks the clause as a general one about any thing whatever, not a statement about one. ἐπιδέχομαι is to admit a thing, to leave room for it. περί τι concedes that the blame need only touch a part.
